distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer clinical disease leaf for spontaneous infection of ascitic fluid without a surgically treatable intra-abdominal source. Cirrhosis acute decompensation, secondary peritonitis, cholangitis, pyelonephritis, organism-specific sepsis, and hepatorenal syndrome remain context, mimic, complication, or future leaves rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking may consume ascites, abdominal pain or tenderness, fever or blunted fever, inflammatory markers, portal-hypertensive ascites context, and initial diagnostic paracentesis cell counts when those are available at presentation. Ascitic culture species, susceptibility, secondary-source exclusion, final adjudication, and treatment response should stay confirmatory/non-ranking unless a post-workup mode explicitly uses them.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Portal-hypertensive ascites with low opsonic defense
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Ascitic fluid formed in portal-hypertensive or severe hepatic dysfunction contexts often has low complement, low protein, impaired opsonic activity, and poor bacterial clearance. This is the permissive fluid compartment for SBP, not the cirrhosis leaf itself.

Portal-systemic shunting, impaired Kupffer-cell clearance, neutrophil dysfunction, low complement, malnutrition, alcohol-associated immune dysfunction, malignancy, diabetes, or immunosuppression reduce containment of translocated organisms.

Gut dysbiosis, bowel edema, slowed motility, increased permeability, GI bleeding, proton-pump inhibitor exposure, hospitalization, or antibiotic pressure allow enteric bacteria to cross the intestinal barrier and reach mesenteric nodes, blood, and ascitic fluid.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Viable bacterial burden in ascitic fluid
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Monomicrobial infection of ascitic fluid by enteric gram-negative bacilli, streptococci, enterococci, or less common organisms. Burden drives culture positivity and sustains peritoneal inflammation when antibiotic coverage is inactive.

Bacterial PAMPs in ascites trigger local complement, cytokine, macrophage, and neutrophil recruitment, producing ascitic PMN elevation, abdominal pain, tenderness, ileus, and sometimes peritoneal signs.
Peritoneal infection and bacteremia risk drive IL-6, TNF, IL-1, acute-phase response, fever or blunted fever, leukocyte changes, CRP/procalcitonin rise, tachycardia, and malaise.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Hemodynamic, renal, and hepatic decompensation cascade
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Inflammation in decompensated liver disease worsens vasodilation, effective arterial underfilling, capillary leak, renal hypoperfusion, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, shock physiology, and death risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Antimicrobial mismatch or resistant/unusual pathogen activity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Nosocomial acquisition, prior antibiotics, prophylaxis, enterococci, Listeria, resistant gram-negatives, or rare organisms can make standard beta-lactam coverage inactive and prolong ascitic bacterial burden.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Low oncotic pressure and liver disease support ascites formation.
Ascitic PMNs are a major component of elevated ascitic leukocytes in SBP.
Neutrophilic ascitic inflammation raises both the total ascitic leukocyte count and the neutrophil fraction, keeping the WBC/PMN/fraction covariance triangle numerically coherent.
Higher neutrophil fraction raises absolute PMN count for a given total cell count.
Peritoneal neutrophilic inflammation often produces abdominal pain but can be asymptomatic.
Tenderness generally tracks local peritoneal inflammation.
Fever and CRP often rise together, but cirrhosis can blunt fever.
Peripheral leukocytosis and CRP are shared systemic inflammatory outputs.
Creatinine rise is the observed renal injury signal.
Renal failure strongly worsens SBP survival.
Shock or severe circulatory failure increases early mortality.
Encephalopathy marks low reserve and aspiration/ICU risk.
Active therapy lowers persistent infection and complication hazards.

treatments.treatment_name: Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic cell count and culture

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Paracentesis is meaningful when ascites is present.
Listeria, enterococcus, or resistant gram-negative contexts can fail cephalosporins.
Renal impairment changes dosing and toxicity.
Effect depends on susceptible Listeria or enterococcus context.
Ampicillin becomes relevant when cephalosporin-inactive pathogens are plausible.
Renal impairment raises toxicity and dosing complexity.
Renal dysfunction increases potential renal-protective value.
Albumin can worsen pulmonary edema or overload in vulnerable patients.

treatments.treatment_name: Repeat paracentesis for nonresponse or uncertain source

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Persistent PMN elevation suggests nonresponse, mismatch, or secondary-source evaluation.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises baseline susceptibility by providing ascitic substrate and low hepatic reserve.
Low protein ascites lowers local bacterial clearance.
GI bleeding and healthcare exposure increase translocation and resistant/unusual pathogen probability.
Alcohol-associated liver disease can worsen immune dysfunction and reserve without becoming part of the SBP disease name.
Diabetes increases infection susceptibility and worsens reserve while serum glucose remains background-context physiology.
Immunosuppression increases unusual pathogens and can blunt inflammatory expression.
Older or multimorbid hosts can be afebrile and have higher complication risk.
Renal dysfunction shifts SBP toward high mortality and constrains antibiotic/albumin decisions.

supportive_care: Treat this as a pure first-layer SBP leaf: ascitic fluid infection without a surgically treatable intra-abdominal source. Cirrhosis decompensation, organism identity, secondary peritonitis, cholangitis, pyelonephritis, organism-specific sepsis, and hepatorenal syndrome remain context, mimic, complication, or future leaves.
Do not hard-code culture species or susceptibility into presentation-only diagnosis ranking. Culture and susceptibility should modulate treatment once available.

Use diagnostic paracentesis cell count when it is available at presentation; culture species, secondary-source exclusion, final adjudication, and response to antibiotics remain confirmatory/non-ranking unless testing post-workup mode.

Evaluate secondary peritonitis when polymicrobial culture, very high protein/LDH, very low glucose, free air, abscess, focal surgical abdomen, or poor PMN decline suggests a surgically treatable source.
Renal protection, volume status, albumin use, vasopressors, and ICU monitoring should be driven by renal, circulatory, and respiratory axes rather than a fixed treatment label.
Reassess active antibiotic coverage if PMN count, fever, pain, renal dysfunction, or inflammatory markers fail to improve.
quality_notes: No treatment-rank or expected-diagnosis label fields are encoded.
Organism identity and secondary-source exclusion are intentionally modeled as context or confirmatory workup, not part of the disease name.
